quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: OPS, bags, maunds, yield, waste and noil — the vocabulary of spinning calculations.

questions.q: What does OPS stand for in spinning production?
options: Output per spindle per shift, in ounces
questions.explain: OPS is ounces per spindle per shift — the standard way of quoting ring-frame production. Multiply by spindles and shifts to get daily output.

questions.q: As the yarn count (Ne) becomes finer, OPS:
options: Rises in proportion to the count
questions.explain: The table goes from 28.5 OPS at count 6 to 0.9 at count 120 CM: a finer yarn has less weight per length and needs more twist, so each spindle delivers far fewer ounces.

questions.q: In the lecture a 'bag' of yarn weighs 100 lb.
questions.explain: Bags per frame are found by dividing ounces by 16 to get pounds and then by 100 to get bags of 100 lb.

questions.q: A maund, as used for buying cotton in the lecture, is:
questions.explain: Cotton is bought per maund of 37.34 kg (about 82.3 lb). 100 lb is a bag of yarn.

questions.q: What does 'yield' mean in the cotton cost worksheet?
options: The profit per lb of yarn
The fraction of the cotton bought that becomes yarn
The price of waste as a fraction of cotton price
questions.explain: Yield is the share of raw cotton that ends up as yarn (82 % carded, 74 % combed in the sheet); the rest leaves as waste and, for combed yarn, noil.

questions.q: In the combing process, what is noil?
options: The hard waste from the ring frame
Short fibres removed by the comber, about 8 % of the cotton, which sell well
The sizing material added in weaving
The packing material of a bag
questions.explain: Combing removes short fibres as noil. The lecture stresses that noil is worth far more than ordinary waste, which is why the combed formula treats it separately.

questions.q: In the OPS table, what does 'CM' after a count mean?
questions.explain: CM marks combed counts (20 CM, 40 CM, … 120 CM); the plain counts are carded.

questions.q: Waste from carded spinning sells for roughly the same price per lb as the raw cotton.
questions.explain: The sheet credits waste at only 15 % of the cotton price; it is noil that fetches a good price (70 % of cotton price in the sheet).

questions.q: Why is the cotton cost per lb of yarn higher than the cotton cost per lb of cotton?
options: Because yarn is sold in bags
Because only part of each lb of cotton becomes yarn, so each lb of yarn needs more than a lb of cotton
Because cotton is bought in maunds
questions.explain: At 82 % yield a lb of yarn needs 1 ÷ 0.82 = 1.22 lb of cotton, so cost per lb of yarn = cotton cost per lb ÷ yield before any credit for waste.

questions.q: Which of these is the 'subtle point' the lecture draws from the original worksheet?
options: Combed yarn has a lower yield only because the comber is slow
The carded formula credits waste on (1 − yield) while the combed formula separates waste from noil because noil is worth far more
OPS should be measured per day, not per shift
Cotton price should be quoted per kg
questions.explain: The lesson is to ask what each by-product sells for: lumping noil in with waste would understate the credit for combed yarn.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The chain of formulas from spindles to bags and from maund price to adjusted cotton cost.

questions.q: Bags per frame per day are calculated as:
questions.explain: Spindles × shifts × OPS gives ounces per day; ÷ 16 converts to lb and ÷ 100 to bags: 480 × 3 × 28 ÷ 1,600 = 25.2 bags.

questions.q: A frame has 480 spindles and runs 3 shifts a day. How many ounces does it produce per day at 1 OPS?
questions.explain: 480 spindles × 1 oz × 3 shifts = 1,440 oz per day.

questions.q: A frame makes 1,440 oz per day at 1 OPS. How many 100 lb bags is that?
questions.explain: 1,440 ÷ 16 = 90 lb; ÷ 100 = 0.9 bags. Multiply this by the OPS of the count spun to get bags per frame per day.

questions.q: If the OPS of the count spun doubles, bags per frame per day:
questions.explain: Bags per day = 0.9 × OPS for a 480-spindle, 3-shift frame, so production is directly proportional to OPS.

questions.q: Cotton cost per lb is found from the maund price by:
questions.explain: A maund is 37.34 kg, which is 37.34 × 2.2046 ≈ 82.3 lb; dividing the maund price by this gives Rs per lb. Dividing by 37.34 alone gives Rs per kg.

questions.q: Cotton cost per lb of yarn before any waste credit equals:
options: Cotton cost per lb + waste value
questions.explain: Each lb of yarn needs 1 ÷ yield lb of cotton: 34.02 ÷ 0.82 = Rs 41.49 for carded yarn. Multiplying by the yield would wrongly make yarn cheaper than cotton.

questions.q: In the lecture's worksheet, the rupee value of waste is (1 − yield) × cotton cost per lb × proceeds fraction, and it is subtracted from the cotton cost per lb of yarn.
questions.explain: Carded: 0.18 × 34.02 × 0.15 = Rs 0.92, giving 41.49 − 0.92 = Rs 40.57 adjusted cost. For combed yarn the waste and the noil are credited separately.

questions.q: For combed yarn the sheet finds the noil percentage as:
questions.explain: Everything that is not yarn or ordinary waste is noil: 1 − 0.74 − 0.18 = 0.08, i.e. 8 %.

questions.q: If the yield of carded yarn falls from 82 % to 80 % with the same cotton price, the cotton cost per lb of yarn (before waste credit):
options: Rises, because more cotton is needed per lb of yarn
questions.explain: Cost = 34.02 ÷ 0.80 = Rs 42.53 instead of Rs 41.49, a rise of about 2.5 % (not exactly 2 %, because the yield is in the denominator).

questions.q: Which change would reduce the adjusted cotton cost of combed yarn the most, other things equal?
options: A higher selling price for noil
A higher selling price for ordinary waste
questions.explain: Noil is 8 % of the cotton and already sells at 70 % of cotton price, so each extra percentage point of noil proceeds is worth more than the same change on waste at 15 %; OPS and bag weight do not enter the cotton cost.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Bags per frame for different counts, then the cotton cost chain for carded and combed yarn.

questions.q: A 480-spindle frame runs 3 shifts a day spinning count 7 at 28 OPS. How many 100 lb bags does it make per day?
The same 480-spindle, 3-shift frame spins count 30 at 5.5 OPS. How many bags per day?
questions.explain: 0.9 bags at 1 OPS × 5.5 = 4.95 bags per day — about a fifth of the count-7 output.

questions.q: A frame has 1,008 spindles and runs 3 shifts spinning count 24 at 8 OPS. How many 100 lb bags per day?
A mill needs 100 bags a day of count 30 (4.95 bags per frame per day). How many frames does the calculation give, to one decimal place?
questions.explain: 100 ÷ 4.95 = 20.2 frames; in practice the mill installs 21, because 20 would give only 99 bags.

questions.q: Cotton costs Rs 2,800 per maund and a maund is 82.3 lb. What is the cotton cost per lb, to two decimals?
Cotton costs Rs 34.02 per lb and the carded yield is 82 %. What is the cotton cost per lb of carded yarn before any waste credit, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 34.02 ÷ 0.82 = Rs 41.49 per lb of yarn.

questions.q: Carded yield 82 %, cotton Rs 34.02 per lb, waste sold at 15 % of cotton price. Using the worksheet's method (1 − yield) × cotton cost × proceeds fraction, what is the rupee value of waste, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 0.18 × 34.02 × 0.15 = Rs 0.92, which is deducted from Rs 41.49 to give an adjusted carded cost of Rs 40.57.

questions.q: Combed yield is 74 % and cotton costs Rs 34.02 per lb. What is the cotton cost per lb of combed yarn before credits, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 34.02 ÷ 0.74 = Rs 45.97 — Rs 4.48 more than carded because 8 % more cotton leaves as noil.

questions.q: Noil is 8 % of the cotton and sells at 70 % of the Rs 34.02 cotton price. What is the rupee value of noil using the worksheet method, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 0.08 × 34.02 × 0.70 = Rs 1.91 — twice the credit for 18 % of ordinary waste, because noil sells so much better.

questions.q: Doubling the count of a yarn (for example from Ne 20 to Ne 40) roughly halves the bags per frame per day, because the finer yarn is spun more slowly.
questions.explain: Finer counts need more twist per inch and run at lower delivery, so production in bags per frame per day falls sharply as the count rises.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Planning frames, choosing counts and buying cotton in a spinning mill.

questions.q: A mill switches a frame from count 20 (10.3 OPS) to count 40 combed (4.15 OPS). What happens to its daily output in bags?
options: It doubles because the count doubles
It falls to about 40 % of the previous output
It stays the same because spindles are unchanged
questions.explain: Bags are proportional to OPS: 4.15 ÷ 10.3 = 0.40. Finer yarn sells at a higher price per lb, which must compensate for the lower weight produced.

questions.q: A marketing manager quotes yarn prices per lb using the cotton cost per lb of cotton (Rs 34.02) rather than per lb of yarn. What is the result?
options: Prices are too low, because the yield (and waste) has been ignored — carded yarn actually needs Rs 40.57 of cotton per lb
Prices are correct for combed yarn
No effect, because waste is sold
questions.explain: Each lb of yarn consumes 1.22 lb of cotton at 82 % yield; quoting on the raw cotton price under-recovers about Rs 6.5 per lb even after the waste credit.

questions.q: If the cotton price rises from Rs 2,800 to Rs 3,000 per maund, the adjusted cotton cost per lb of yarn rises by roughly the same percentage.
questions.explain: Every line of the sheet — cost per lb, cost per lb of yarn, waste and noil credits — is proportional to the cotton price, so a 7.1 % rise in maund price gives about a 7.1 % rise in adjusted cost.

questions.q: A buyer reports the mill's noil is being sold with the ordinary waste at 15 % of cotton price. What should the costing office do?
options: Point out that noil sells at around 70 % of cotton price and that selling it separately lowers the adjusted cost of combed yarn
questions.explain: The lecture's subtle point: noil is a valuable by-product. Credited at 15 % instead of 70 %, the combed yarn's cotton cost would look about Rs 1.50 per lb higher than it should.

questions.q: A mill has 20 frames of 480 spindles running 3 shifts and an order for 50 bags a day of count 20 (10.3 OPS). Can it meet the order?
options: No — it makes only 9.27 bags a day
Yes — 20 frames give about 185 bags a day, so 6 frames are enough
questions.explain: One frame gives 0.9 × 10.3 = 9.27 bags; 50 ÷ 9.27 = 5.4, so 6 frames meet the order and 20 frames would make 185 bags.

questions.q: Which figure should a planner use to estimate the cotton to buy for 1,000 bags of carded yarn at 82 % yield?
options: 100,000 lb ÷ 0.82 ≈ 121,951 lb of cotton, about 1,482 maunds
questions.explain: Cotton needed = yarn ÷ yield = 121,951 lb; ÷ 82.3 lb per maund ≈ 1,482 maunds. Multiplying by the yield is the classic reversal error.

questions.q: A mill is deciding between spinning count 20 carded (10.3 OPS) and 20 CM combed (10.5 OPS). Which statement is right?
options: Combed 20s gives slightly more bags per frame but costs more in cotton per lb because of the lower yield
Combed 20s gives fewer bags and cheaper cotton
Both give identical output and cost
questions.explain: The table shows 10.5 OPS against 10.3 (combed sliver spins slightly better), but combed yield is 74 % against 82 %, so the cotton cost per lb of yarn is higher even after the noil credit.

questions.q: Running a fourth shift is a way to raise bags per frame per day beyond the 3-shift figure in the lecture.
questions.explain: A day has 24 hours and three 8-hour shifts already fill it; output can rise only through more spindles, higher OPS (coarser count or faster spindles) or better efficiency.

questions.q: The waste proceeds fraction falls from 15 % to 10 % because waste prices drop. For carded yarn at Rs 34.02 per lb cotton and 82 % yield, the adjusted cost:
options: Rises by about Rs 0.31 per lb
Falls by about Rs 0.31 per lb
questions.explain: Waste credit falls from 0.18 × 34.02 × 0.15 = 0.92 to 0.18 × 34.02 × 0.10 = 0.61, so the adjusted cost rises by Rs 0.31 per lb.

questions.q: The mid-term review asks for the cost of yarn, but the worksheet gives only the cotton cost. What is still missing for a full yarn cost?
options: Nothing — cotton is the whole cost
Conversion cost (power, labour, depreciation per lb), packing and margin, which are stacked on top of the cotton cost
questions.explain: Adjusted cotton cost is only the first layer; the next lecture (Simple Yarn Costing) adds conversion, packing and margin to reach a selling price.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that chain the production and cost formulas and expose the usual slips.

questions.q: A 480-spindle frame runs 3 shifts on count 60 combed at 2.6 OPS for 25 working days. How many bags does it make in the month?
questions.explain: Per day 0.9 × 2.6 = 2.34 bags; × 25 days = 58.5 bags a month.

questions.q: A student calculates bags per frame as 480 × 3 × 28 ÷ 100 = 403 bags a day. What was forgotten?
options: Dividing by 16 to convert ounces to pounds
questions.explain: 40,320 oz must first be divided by 16 to give 2,520 lb; ÷ 100 then gives 25.2 bags, not 403.

questions.q: Cotton is bought at Rs 3,000 per maund (82.3 lb). With carded yield 82 % and waste credited at 15 % of cotton price on (1 − yield), what is the adjusted carded cotton cost per lb of yarn, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Cotton Rs 36.45 per lb; ÷ 0.82 = 44.45; waste credit 0.18 × 36.45 × 0.15 = 0.98; adjusted = Rs 43.47.

questions.q: Adjusted cotton cost is Rs 40.57 per lb for carded and Rs 43.15 for combed yarn. How many rupees more cotton cost does a 100 lb bag of combed yarn carry?
questions.explain: 2.58 × 100 = Rs 258 per bag — before the extra conversion cost of combing.

questions.q: The worksheet's waste credit is computed on (1 − yield) lb of waste per lb of cotton, but then subtracted from a cost expressed per lb of yarn. Strictly, what should the credit per lb of yarn be?
options: (1 − yield) ÷ yield × cotton cost × proceeds fraction, i.e. 0.92 ÷ 0.82 ≈ Rs 1.12
questions.explain: Each lb of yarn comes from 1 ÷ 0.82 lb of cotton, which produces 0.18 ÷ 0.82 = 0.22 lb of waste; 0.22 × 34.02 × 0.15 = Rs 1.12. The worksheet's simpler version slightly understates the credit — a point worth checking in the original.

questions.q: How many lb of raw cotton are needed to make one 100 lb bag of combed yarn at 74 % yield, to one decimal?
questions.explain: 100 ÷ 0.74 = 135.1 lb of cotton, of which 18 lb becomes waste and 8 lb noil.

questions.q: At 1 OPS, two frames of 240 spindles each produce the same daily ounces as one frame of 480 spindles on the same shifts.
questions.explain: Production depends on total spindles × shifts × OPS; 2 × 240 × 3 = 480 × 3 = 1,440 oz a day.

questions.q: A mill wants 10 bags a day from one 480-spindle frame running 3 shifts. What OPS is required, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Bags = 0.9 × OPS, so OPS = 10 ÷ 0.9 = 11.11 — roughly count 18 (11 OPS) in the table.

questions.q: Combed yield is 74 % and noil is 8 %. A student takes waste as 1 − 0.74 = 26 % and credits all of it at 15 %. Compared with the worksheet, the student's adjusted combed cost is:
options: Too low, because noil was credited at 15 % instead of 70 %? No — too high, because the valuable noil was credited at only 15 %
Too high, because the 8 % of noil was credited at 15 % instead of 70 %
Too low, because waste was over-credited
questions.explain: The student's credit is 0.26 × 34.02 × 0.15 = Rs 1.33 against the worksheet's 0.92 + 1.91 = Rs 2.83, so the adjusted cost comes out Rs 1.50 too high.

questions.q: Using the OPS table, a 480-spindle 3-shift frame spins count 10 (22 OPS). By how many bags per day does its output exceed the same frame on count 40 CM (4.15 OPS)?
questions.explain: 19.8 − 3.735 = 16.07 bags a day: the same frame makes more than five times the weight on the coarse count.
